data.title: Bratislava – Brezalauspurc, a Great Moravian hillfort above the Danube ford
data.excerpt: The Bratislava hillfort is one of only three Great Moravian sites named directly in the chronicles of the 9th and 10th centuries — as Brezalauspurc, beneath which the Magyars crushed the Bavarian army on 4 July 907. The castle hill yielded a timber-and-earth rampart, a small stone palace and one of the largest buildings of 9th-century Great Moravia; a well in the settlement below held the skeletons of seven men who died a violent death and a wreath of 13 axe-shaped currency bars.
data.metaTitle: Brezalauspurc – the Great Moravian hillfort in Bratislava
data.metaDescription: The Great Moravian hillfort of Brezalauspurc, scene of the battle near Bratislava in 907, named in 9th–10th-century chronicles and on a coin of King Stephen.

children.text: The Bratislava hillfort is one of the three hillforts — or rather the three settlement and militarily important sites of the Great Moravian period (Nitrava, Dowina, Brezalauspurc) — which found their way directly into the chronicles of the 9th and 10th centuries. This is documented, for example, by the chronicle of Aventinus, where the battle between the Magyars and the Bavarians in 907 is described as the battle at Braslavespurch. The Salzburg Annals record it as the battle at Brezaluspurc, and the coin of King Stephen from the year 1000 bears the legend P (or B) reslavva civ in its circular inscription. The origin of the name is usually derived from the magnate Preslav or Breslav, to whom the hillfort probably belonged.

The nearby ford across the Danube was already an important strategic point in earlier periods, and it was duly protected from the “castle hill”. On the foundations of earlier structures the Slavs built an important centre whose prominent landmark in the later period was a basilica (church). The hillfort was surrounded by a rampart along its entire circuit.
Before the rise of Great Moravia

blocks.caption: An artist's impression of the appearance of the Bratislava hillfort in the time of Great Moravia
blocks.alt: An artist's impression of the appearance of the Bratislava hillfort in the time of Great Moravia

children.text: Within the territory of Bratislava we have so far no hillfort documented that could be safely assigned to the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon, that is, to the period before the rise of Great Moravia. Occupation of the castle hill in the 8th century is, however, indicated by a fragment of a die for embossing a circular plaque, which, as Štefanovičová notes, could be assigned to this chronological horizon on the basis of its decoration. The die bears a figural scene showing a horseman with a human figure lying beneath the horse's hooves. The figures stand out in relief from a flat punched background. They are executed to a high artistic standard. Archaeologists interpret the relief as a depiction of triumph over a defeated enemy. The find thus indicates the presence of a metalworker on the Bratislava castle hill; unfortunately, we as yet know no further evidence of his activity. The embossing die was found north of the present-day castle palace, in the area between the former castle ditch and the amphitheatre. Several fragments of vessels were also found at the castle which, by their manner of manufacture, are assigned to the 8th century. This suggests the possibility that the castle hill was occupied in an earlier period than the 9th century, when it became one of the important fortified centres of Great Moravia.
The Great Moravian hillfort — the course and construction of the defences

The hillfort of the Great Moravian period was fortified by a massive rampart, in the greater part with a timber construction only. This was documented by the excavation along the circuit of the eastern lower terrace of the castle complex, where a not entirely identical construction was identified at two points. In the trench in the park, beneath a fairly thick medieval fill, a burnt layer of soil was encountered, under which a timber chamber built of thick oak beams without iron nails was uncovered. The chamber was open towards the interior of the hillfort; it consisted of two side walls and a front wall, and its surviving height was 250 cm. The timber beams were decayed but not burnt, so this was not a deliberate firing; only the upper part had probably been affected by fire. In this section of the defences no rebuilding could be observed. Judging by the front wall of the chamber, the fortification ran along the contour line parallel to the later Gothic stone wall, only shifted about 5 m into the interior of the enclosure.

In the northern part the situation was somewhat different. A thick burnt layer appeared here, which also spread towards the interior of the hillfort and reached as much as 2 m. It was very strongly fired, in places with parts of slag burnt to a vitrified state, which, however, was not chemically determined under the conditions of the time. In its lower part the timber construction was built as smaller chambers, as in the previous case; the upper part had a grillage construction filled with earth. In the northern part of the trench a square stone tower was set into the timber rampart, of which the western inner part survived. Its poured masonry reached a thickness of 2 m and the length of the wall was 10 m. The outer side was evidently demolished during the construction of the Gothic defences at the end of the 14th century. The tower did not reach the base of the timber-and-earth rampart; the rampart's front wall was identified even beneath the tower's foundation masonry. It was one of the defensive towers with which the outer defences were strengthened in the 13th century, while the original timber-and-earth construction was retained and used. It was originally built in the 9th century, and later, sometime in the 11th century, its upper part was rebuilt as a grillage construction. It is interesting to note that in this section the front of the fortification consisted only of a timber front wall, which was not strengthened by a stone wall, even though there was no shortage of stone in the immediate vicinity. The walls of Great Moravian defences were often protected on the outer side by a stone wall, and not only where stone lay close at hand, as at the hillforts of Devínska Kobyla or at Neštich near Svätý Jur, where the natural setting was similar, but also, for example, in the floodplain at Mikulčice, where the stone had to be brought in. Remains of a timber construction, without the possibility of detailed excavation, were identified on the northern side of the castle complex, beneath the outer wall of the defences of the Luginsland bastion. They showed as a red fired layer and pieces of charred beams. An exceptionally well-preserved timber construction was found in the cellar of the western part of the Luginsland wing, where it reached a depth of as much as 6 m. Since this was a construction trench dug after the official end of the excavation, it was not possible to examine or document the construction. It consisted of exceptionally well-preserved large oak beams which had charred naturally. Traces of a burnt layer with timber fragments of beams were also identified beneath part of the western defences and thus made it possible to reconstruct the probable course of the fortification, which on the eastern, northern and western sides essentially follows the configuration of the terrain in the same way as the later Gothic walls.

blocks.caption: Ground plan of the hillfort in the 9th century after Štefanovičová
blocks.alt: Ground plan of the hillfort in the 9th century after Štefanovičová

children.text: On the southern side the castle hill fell away steeply, and the fortification here ran in a S–N direction towards the crown tower of the present-day palace. Its upper part had
a grillage construction, whose outer side was strengthened by a wall of quarry stone bonded with clay

. It was 1 m thick, and in some sections the beams of the fortification were set into it. Interesting is the situation identified by a small deep trench, which perhaps indicates older masonry beneath the fortification. The course of the rampart towards the crown tower could still be traced, at least indistinctly, west of the wing of the court of honour and also at the foundations of the crown tower, inside the terrace added to the palace during a later medieval alteration. At present we in fact know the entire course of the timber-and-earth defences, which probably date from the beginning of the 9th century and were used, with several rebuildings, until the end of the 14th century, when they were replaced by Gothic stone walls. The fortification was for its time very massive and effective; we also know from historical sources that it withstood various attacks during military clashes on several occasions, especially in the 11th century.

blocks.caption: Reconstruction of the defensive wall in the 9th century
blocks.alt: Reconstruction of the defensive wall in the 9th century

children.text: Buildings on the hillfort

The area inside the fortification had its own natural division in height, which it was possible to reconstruct from various height measurements taken during the excavation. The highest part lay beneath the western half of the present-day palace, from where the ground gradually fell away and in the east ran out as a tongue into a smaller terrace. In the 9th century this configuration was used to erect the most important buildings on its summit. On the highest part the excavation
identified the foundations and part of the above-foundation masonry of a small stone palace

, which had an elongated ground plan oriented W–E. It was built of quarry stone bonded with clay, with dressed stone blocks used for the corners. Its walls were faced, it was plastered on the inside and divided by a partition into two rooms. The southern wall has not survived; it was lost during the construction of the Gothic palace. In the northern part an entrance opening with part of a stone pavement was identified. Owing to the fragmentary state of the find, no heating installation could be located. Its dating to the 9th century is assumed on the basis of its ground plan and its relationship to the other structures discovered in the immediate vicinity. The dimensions of the feature can only be estimated at 12 × 5.5 m. It may be assumed that this was a single-storey palace of the 9th century.

blocks.caption: A possible appearance of the basilica at the hillfort
blocks.alt: A possible appearance of the basilica at the hillfort

children.text: East of it, on the descending tongue of ground,
a smaller dwelling feature

was discovered in the cellar beneath the south-eastern tower of the present-day palace. It had a stone footing of quarry stone laid in clay, the interior space was finished with yellow sandy clay, and at the north-eastern corner traces of a fired hearth with an indication of a stone surround were identified. Its northern wall survived to a length of 4 m, together with parts of the western and eastern walls. The southern one was destroyed during the medieval rebuilding, when the Gothic palace was erected. The feature produced finds of sherds of pottery, mostly wheel-thrown and decorated with wavy lines, which can be assigned to the 9th century. This was evidently a dwelling which had a timber log building standing on a stone footing. Few similar buildings of the 9th century have been found; at that time the prevailing simple dwelling was a semi-sunken building — a dwelling with its floor sunk into a pit — or a post-built structure. Similar buildings come from other centres of power of Great Moravia, for example from Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště. In the case of the dwelling at Bratislava Castle this is unquestionably a stone footing for a log-built dwelling.
The basilica

The remains of a church building on the eastern spur of the upper terrace undoubtedly rank among the most important finds at the Bratislava hillfort. Part of the structure of a church was identified there, which at the south-western corner was overlain by a tower structure, probably in the 10th century, and was then overlain again, together with a tower structure in the same section, by a new church building of the 11th century. The superimposition of three masonry structures bonded with different, visually distinguishable mortars, and the fortunate circumstance of the discovery of a grave beneath the 11th-century wall which contained a characteristic Great Moravian
gombík

, provided the key to dating the buildings. The oldest building phase consisted of the perimeter wall of the southern aisle and of the south-western front, and of three pairs of massive piers which divided the interior into three aisles. The walls, and above all the piers, were built of dressed stone blocks; in some cases architectural elements or stones with carved Roman inscriptions (FECIT VERIAN) were reused as building material. Roman bricks or their fragments were also used in abundance in the masonry. For the most part they originally belonged to a building of the XIIII Roman legion, whose stamps survive on them; the material came from an unidentified Roman building somewhere in the vicinity. Given its quantity, we assume that the building may have stood directly on the castle hill. Similar situations are common at other places in Bratislava too. Within the castle complex the only indication so far of a stone building older than the 9th century was a small part of a wall visible only from the side beneath the tower structure of the 10th century. Its excavation, however, could not be carried out for technical reasons, and so this question remains open. The said remains of the 9th-century building form only a torso of the whole ground plan. The northern perimeter masonry has not survived, and above all the eastern part of the church, which makes it impossible to judge what the sanctuary looked like. The surviving perimeter wall and the pairs of piers were oriented E–W. Inside, the building was plastered and decorated with paintings which most probably depicted figural scenes. The colours of the paintings were earthy — ochre, yellow, brown-red — and framed by broad grey bands. Fragments of plaster with paintings were found mainly beside the piers of the nave. In 1990, during a rescue excavation west of the wing of the court of honour, a quantity of Roman building material and plaster with identical painting was found dumped in a secondary position. This was evidently part of the masonry moved after the demolition of the church. Details of the surviving plaster indicate that it came from windows and the framing of entrances, and help to complete the picture of its appearance.

The basilica was probably built by two groups of craftsmen. The first, probably inexperienced with a building of this type, erected the stone walls rather irregularly, without a right-angled system. The second group of builders completed the church and plastered the surface of the masonry with a levelling mortar, which formed the base for a finer plaster with fresco decoration.

Its classification as a sacred building is indicated by its layout itself, its eastern orientation and the graves which lay around it. The custom of burying beside a church was already common in the 9th century. Since in the 11th century a second church stood on the remains of the older church and was used until the first third of the 13th century, an intensively used cemetery extended around the buildings. From the beginning of the 11th to the beginning of the 13th century the graves in it lay in as many as five layers. This intensive burying probably destroyed part of the older graves, which is why finds of the 9th century are represented only in small numbers. The uncovered graves of the earliest horizon lay on the southern side of the building; one was placed to the west. They contained jewellery which undoubtedly belongs to the circle of Great Moravian jewellery, and of a kind used only among the higher-ranking classes. These were earrings decorated with a pendant in the form of a bunch of grapes, known as grape-cluster earrings, earrings with small spheres decorated on the surface with tiny grains — granulation — and also simple ring earrings. All of them were of silver. Another striking ornament were
gombíky
, which were probably used more as an ornament than for fastening clothing. They were hollow, joined from two hemispheres of sheet bronze and decorated with an engraved geometric ornament.

The dating of the remains of the church building depends to a large extent on the associated finds, because the building itself has no architectural details that would allow it to be dated. This situation is similar at other sites with finds of sacred architecture in the area of Great Moravia. On the basis of the grave finds made around the oldest building at the Bratislava hillfort, its construction can be assumed to have taken place around the middle of the 9th century. With its three-aisled layout and an overall width of 13 m, it ranks among the largest buildings of the 9th century in the area of Great Moravia. We do not know its length, nor do we know what termination it had in the east. The thickness of the perimeter wall was around 90 cm, and the piers measured approximately 100 × 100 cm. The articulation of the walls with antae and the three-aisled layout, as well as the overall dimensions, bring the Bratislava building closest to the three-aisled Basilica of St John the Baptist uncovered at Zalavár in the locality known as Réceskút. This also indicates the route by which the builders, or the architectural inspiration for both buildings, probably came, that is, from the Dalmatian region. In the architecture there both the overall layout of the building and the articulation of the walls with antae are common, and written sources also suggest that this current of Christianising activity is very probable.

children.text: The basilica came to an end at some point in the course of the 10th century, when a fortification with a masonry tower was built over its southern part. This fortification was to protect only the upland part of the hillfort, but it was probably never completed.

On the basis of the finds described above, Bratislava Castle can be regarded as an important Great Moravian fortress which was the ecclesiastical as well as the secular centre of a wider region. The prince's retinue, and probably also a church dignitary, resided there. The castle's important position is also reflected in the fact that its name, as one of the three known names from the area of Great Moravia, was recorded in the Salzburg Annals as Brezalauspurc. The annalist noted briefly that a terrible battle of the Bavarian and Magyar armies took place beneath it on 4 July 907, which ended in the complete defeat of the Bavarians and opened the way west for the Magyars. Probably shortly afterwards, or already at that time, the Bratislava hillfort lost its function for a while, although the Magyars probably did not capture it — at least no indications of this have survived. The castle gained an important role again in the 11th century, when it became a comitatus castle of the Kingdom of Hungary and the seat of members of the royal family.
The settlement below the castle and the area of today's old town in the Great Moravian period

children.text: In contrast to the striking finds on the castle hill, the evidence of occupation below it in the 9th century is far more modest. This is probably caused above all by the extensive later medieval and modern built-up area, which prevents more continuous excavation. At several sites where excavation could be carried out, evidence of life in the Great Moravian period was indeed found, even if only as a fragmentary picture. At many places in the western part of the Old Town a settlement layer was identified, but since no features could be recorded in it, the finds give an idea only of the extent of the inhabited area, not of the character of the occupation.

Directly below the castle, on the eastern slope of the castle hill, part of a fortification dated to the 9th century was identified during excavation near the Church of St Nicholas. Its overall course is not known, but it was probably the fortification of a bailey.

blocks.caption: Typical Great Moravian jewellery from the hillfort
blocks.alt: Typical Great Moravian jewellery from the hillfort

children.text: The settlement below the castle probably began to develop as early as the 9th century and was concentrated in the area between the later western town walls and Ventúrska Street. On the inner side of the town walls, at their north-western corner, a sunken dwelling of the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century was uncovered.
The dwelling was sunk about 70 cm into the ground surface of the time

and had a relatively very well-preserved internal fill. A torso of a charred timber construction survived in it, which allows some constructional details to be reconstructed. The sunken-featured building had a square ground plan with an area of 320 cm².
The walls consisted of split oak beams erected in the classic log technique

, with joints at the north-western and south-western corners; at the north-eastern and south-eastern corners, however, the ends of the beams were set into a groove in a corner post. An oven was placed in the north-eastern corner, which on the outside had clay insulation separating it from the timber construction of the wall. The oven was of stone. Opposite it, in the south-eastern corner, was the entrance opening, above which there was probably a protective porch. The floor was finished with a thin, two-centimetre layer of yellow clayey soil. Only three vessels were found in the dwelling, and it is dated by them. Further settlement finds come from Kapitulská Street 18 and Ventúrska Street 6, but these are only settlement pits, which say little about the layout of the settlement, rather about its extent. So far the finds comprise only pottery material; no evidence of production features or of craft activity has been identified.

blocks.caption: Gombíky from the Bratislava hillfort (P. Dvořák: Stopy dávnej minulosti 3)
blocks.alt: Gombíky from the Bratislava hillfort (P. Dvořák: Stopy dávnej minulosti 3)

children.text: From this point of view the find at Ventúrska Street 3, in the building of the medieval university Academia Istropolitana, is remarkable. In the courtyard formed by several houses, during excavation connected with the repair of the building,
a well was found
, filled in its lower part with ash and charcoal. On this layer
the skeletons of seven adult men had been thrown. At the level of the layer of skeletons there was a discontinuous wreath of 13 iron axe-shaped currency bars around the edge of the well

. On the basis of several fragments of sherds the find was dated no later than the first half of the 10th century. So far, however, it has no parallel even within the Great Moravian horizon. The dumped skeletons of the men testify to their violent death, which may have occurred during some military clash. From this point of view a skirmish at the beginning of the 10th century, which could have been connected with the advance of Magyar war bands, might be considered. It is remarkable that
the men had no weapons or other objects that would allow them to be assigned to a particular social group

. The axe-shaped currency bars, laid irregularly in a wreath around the circumference of the well, are a peculiar object which had the function of certain units of measurement. They also served as a form of currency in the period before coinage was introduced. The name of these objects derives from their shape, which resembles slender long axes with a blade on one side and a butt, including a drilled hole, on the other. The object was, however, too thin and fragile to be used functionally as an axe. Axe-shaped currency bars are often found in larger numbers in hoards, which suggests that they were used to store a raw material that was precious at that time. The greatest concentration in Slovakia is known from the hillfort of Pobedim near Piešťany and its surroundings, where developed smithing was also documented. In the Bratislava area this is so far the only larger find of this kind. Leaving aside the manner in which the currency bars were deposited around the dumped corpses of the men in the well, it is evidence, if not of their manufacture somewhere on the edge of the settlement, then certainly of the trade contacts which the settlement had in the 9th century. Because iron axe-shaped currency bars are characteristic above all of the first half of the 9th century, their find documents a relatively early trading or market settlement below the castle. This explanation is natural in view of the fact that not far below the southern slope of the castle hill there was a ford across the Danube that had been used from time immemorial and was certainly exploited for trading purposes.

blocks.caption: A coin of Stephen I from around the year 1000, which was minted in Bratislava. It bears the inscription (B)reslava Civ
blocks.alt: A coin of Stephen I from around the year 1000, which was minted in Bratislava. It bears the inscription (B)reslava Civ

children.text: The 9th-century settlement in the area between the western town walls and Ventúrska Street had its
cemetery nearby, in the middle part of today's Panská Street
, beneath the Gothic palace of the present-day City Gallery. The group of graves, although small, provides important information for assessing its character.
An iron axe

found in a man's grave belongs to the group known as bearded axes, named after its cut-away body and the fairly high pointed lugs beside the opening for the haft. The butt was elongated and rounded, the blade straight. Axes of this shape are characteristic of the 9th century. In the cemetery
a grave of a man — a warrior, of a woman and of a child
was identified. Judging by the furnishing with grave goods, and especially by the addition of cockerel legs, we may assume that those buried
still adhered to pagan customs

. This is also supported by the grave of a dead person in a crouched position, which testifies that Christianity, which in the 9th century already predominated among the princely class, advanced only slowly among ordinary people.

Besides the settlement below the castle on the eastern slope of the castle hill, which also became the starting point for the later emergence of the medieval town, a small settlement was also recorded at the foot of the southern slope of the hill. During the excavation of the building of the so-called Water Tower
a semi-sunken building set into the ground was also uncovered on the former Vydrická Street
. Pottery finds assign it to the 9th century. The sunken-featured building had a square ground plan and was probably part of a small settlement beside the Danube ford.

The latest finds from the excavation of the Main Square in the Old Town indicate that the settlement beside the western town walls was not the only one. A sunken feature with pottery that can be assigned to the end of the 9th and the beginning of the 10th century shows that there was occupation at the end of the 9th century in this position too, which later became the central part of the medieval town. On the northern side below the castle hill, 9th-century occupation was identified in
a settlement layer beside the Church of the Holy Trinity and at the point where Partizánska Street joins Palisády
. Here, in the courtyard of the former Lutheran Hospital,
a Slavic feature was disturbed
during the reconstruction of a utility network; it contained sherd material of the 9th century.

Denser occupation has been identified in the area between the Bratislava and the Devín hillforts. Besides isolated finds of pottery or hearths (Karlova Ves, the locality known as Kútiky, behind the Botanical Garden), an inhumation cemetery was also identified. In the area of Karlova Ves (on the grounds of the Botanical Garden beside the Vydrica stream) it was uncovered in 1954 by Ľ. Kraskovská. She discovered 15 inhumation graves there. In two graves a lining of the grave with wooden boards was identified. The grave inventory consisted of pottery and ornaments. Earrings were identified with a grape-like cluster above the upper arch, or with granulated wreaths placed opposite each other in the middle of the arch. The pottery, of rather coarse form, was made on a slowly rotating potter's wheel. The cemetery dates from about the middle of the 9th century.
The Celtic oppidum and the Roman burgus

In the courtyard of the castle palace, as well as on the northern terrace of the complex, archaeologists of the City Institute for the Protection of Monuments found the remains of unique structures of the period of the 1st century BC. The finds caused a great stir; in the media they were partly interpreted as the discovery of a treasure. Part of the find were indeed gold coins bearing the legend Biatec. As for the buildings, foreign historians endorsed the dating and agreed that this is the most impressive building north of the Alps from the Late La Tène period.

The Castle was thus in the past the site of the acropolis of one of the most important Celtic hillforts — an oppidum — in Central Europe. “These features were built using Roman building technique and are a unique find not only in terms of their age, but also of their quality. The original interior plaster and poured floors with pebble decoration have survived in them, which have no parallel in Slovakia,” says Štassel.

According to Štassel, the courtyard is full of Roman buildings in a Celtic setting, which have several building phases. The northern terrace of the Castle, beneath which an underground garage is to be built, has several separate Roman buildings which were multi-storeyed. What all the features have in common is, for example, the surviving high-quality poured floors.
